schools.summary: Gill identifies Eliphaz as the oldest of the friends, first to open the dispute, now answering a second time as the course comes round.
Henry hears a man stung: Eliphaz falls foul on Job for not applauding them, the temper of proud disputants who charge crimes on any who will not say as they say.
Clarke lays out the three movements of the speech in advance — impiety (vv.1-13), man's corruption (vv.14-16), the desolation of the wicked (vv.17-35).
Keil and Delitzsch read the interrogative He (cf. ch. 13:25) and take 'east wind' (Hosea 12:2) as worthless, vehement blustering; Ellicott draws the inference that Job is therefore not wise.

Clarke renders 'the science of wind,' fixes 'belly' as the breath-filled cavity, and makes the east wind the stormy kadim of Acts 27:14 — Job's speech a hurricane of words; Wesley calls it pernicious discourse.

Henry hears the charge of folly and absurdity — Job's reputation for wisdom forfeited (as Bildad ch. 8:2, Zophar ch. 11:2) — and reflects on vain knowledge that puffs up and idle talk we must give account for.
Gill grants windy knowledge ill becomes a wise man, but demurs that Job did not in fact utter such vain things.
Gill: only what increases wisdom, grace, and holy living profits; the fit matter of a wise man's mouth is God's word and the experiences of grace.
Clarke sharpens 'unprofitable talk' into irreverence — talking of one's Maker without reverence, sound in the place of sense.
Ellicott: Job's arguments, pretentious and seemingly recondite, are unprofitable and can do no good.
Gill: the grace of fear Job truly had could not be cast off (a covenant gift without repentance); 'fear' may mean the outward form of worship.

Clarke hears Job arraigning providence instead of supplicating; Wesley reads 'makest void fear' as an assault on piety by the principle that God makes no difference between good and bad, banishing prayer as useless.
Ellicott: Job's fatalism (ch. 12:16-25) checks prayer and sets an example toward murmuring and blasphemy.

Henry sums religion as fearing God and praying to him, yet calls the charge 'utterly false though wanting not some colour' — much of it merely inferred from Job's doctrine, an injustice of heated dispute.
Ellicott lays out both constructions of the clause and inclines to 'thine iniquity teacheth thy mouth,' granting the next verse favours the reverse.
Clarke hears the 'tongue of the crafty' as sophistry derived from the serpent (Gen. 3:1), wisdom from beneath; Wesley: impious principles covered with fair pretences of piety.
Gill: the mouth betrays the heart's wickedness; the unbridled tongue makes religion vain (James 1:26).
Henry: worse to teach iniquity than to utter it (Matt. 5:19); good words mixed with bad as tradesmen mix their wares — honesty the best policy.

debates.question: Which way is 'thy mouth uttereth thine iniquity' to be construed?

sides.position: the mouth proclaims/teaches the iniquity the crafty tongue tries to conceal
the iniquity within teaches the mouth its eloquence, and so chooses the crafty tongue

schools.summary: Gill relishes the courtroom figure: Job's own lips are judge, jury, and witness, instead of a thousand witnesses, sparing Eliphaz the sentence.
Henry grants the self-condemnation but denies the fairness — the friends provoked Job to the words they now use against him (Titus 3:11; Luke 19:22).
Keil and Delitzsch turn to the coming taunt: the sarcasm assumes the first-created man had the deepest insight (Schlottmann's Hindu proverb), and reject 'wast thou born as the first man.'

themes: prelude to the taunt of antiquity

schools.summary: Ellicott reads the taunt as a retort on ch. 12:2ff., where Job claimed the creation itself could teach; Keil and Delitzsch supply the premise that the first man, born before the world was formed, had deepest insight.
Clarke: 'Wert thou born before Adam?' — it ill becomes the fallen child of a fallen parent to talk as Job does.
Gill: does Job imagine himself the first Adam, created in wisdom, or that he has lived through all the ages gathering knowledge?
Henry: Job's modest claim of equal understanding (ch. 12:3) is twisted into a pretension to be senior to Adam and made before the hills like Wisdom (Prov. 8:23).
Keil and Delitzsch look ahead to the 'consolations of God' as the friends' majestic promises and gloss 'gently' by the soft-flowing laat of Isa. 8:6.
Clarke hears strong sarcasm: wert thou in the celestial cabinet when God said 'Let us make man'? dost thou alone have wisdom?
Gill: only the Son was truly in the Father's council, yet God does reveal the secrets of his love and covenant to them that fear him.
Henry: does Job pretend to the cabinet-council of heaven? there are secret things that belong not to us.

themes: sarcasm at pretended intimacy with God

schools.summary: Gill notes the taunt throws Job's own words (ch. 13:2) back at him — parity of knowledge turned into a charge of presumption.
Clarke: is Job's intellect greater or better cultivated than theirs? let him show one point of knowledge they lack.
Henry: eager disputants think they may commend themselves and disparage opponents; how natural such replies, how simple they look on review.

themes: what knowest thou that we know not

schools.summary: Gill: gray hairs an emblem of wisdom; Eliphaz claims the greater antiquity against Job's hint that wisdom lay with him.
Clarke cites the Chaldee naming Eliphaz the hoary-headed, Bildad the long-lived, Zophar older than Job's father; Eliphaz the eldest, takes the lead.
Henry: 'the fathers on our side' is soon said, not soon proved; against it he sets Ps. 119:100 and Elihu's word (ch. 32:9) that the aged are not always wise.
Wesley reads the comforts as those offered on condition of repentance, now scorned; Clarke spreads a whole array of divergent ancient renderings and bids the reader choose.
Gill: the friends' promises called 'consolations of God' as given in his name, but truly divine comforts are great things Job is charged with slighting.
Ellicott owns the phrase obscure, grants the AV good sense, and glosses 'small with thee' as 'too small for thee.'
Henry: the consolations of God are not small in themselves, but the friends were miserable comforters — the fault lay in their misapplication.

outliers.note: Assembles a long catalogue of mutually contradictory renderings (Vulgate, Syriac, Arabic, Septuagint, Houbigant, Coverdale, Chaldee) and, unusually, declines to decide, leaving the reader to choose.

schools.summary: Clarke sees a furious rolling of the eyes (Rosenmüller: 'what mean thy rolling eyes?'), Job transported beyond himself; Wesley reads the winking as an angry, supercilious look.
Gill: the deceitful heart carries even good men away, drawn of their own lust (James 1:14).
Ellicott: 'why do they wink,' as if Job alone perceived it; Keil and Delitzsch carry the strophe on toward 'what is man that he should be clean.'
Henry frames it as opposition to God, an unkind construction put on a sufferer's distraction.

themes: marks of anguish read as pride

schools.summary: Gill marks the advance: not against men now but against God himself, stretching out the hand — the image the next verses draw out.
Henry protests the want of charity: to read a tempted saint's words as blasphemy (cf. Ps. 73:9) is to give the cause on Satan's side.
Keil and Delitzsch keep the stress on the outward sign — the words let go from the mouth by which Eliphaz presumes to read the heart.

themes: the searcher of hearts who judged otherwise

schools.summary: Ellicott calls it the ceaseless burden of the book (ch. 4:17; 9:2; 25:4); Keil and Delitzsch render the flat impossibility that man born of woman be sinless.
Gill: the question is put by way of contempt to lessen man; clean only through the grace of God and the blood of Christ.
Clarke fixes enosh as weak, dying, miserable man, natural birth reckoned a defilement, and would render 'that he should justify himself.'
Henry grants the doctrine — Job said the same at ch. 14:4 — but denies the inference that Job is therefore a hypocrite; born again of the Spirit, a man is clean.

themes: what is man that he should be clean

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch take the 'holy ones' as the angels, beings of light (ch. 4:18), and refuse to flatten 'the heavens' into a synonym; Ellicott cross-refers ch. 4:18.
Wesley: the saints are angels (Deut. 33:2; Ps. 103:20), pure from corruption but not from imperfection; Clarke: nothing immutable but God, all creaturely goodness derived and dependent.
Gill: God trusts his saints with much but not with themselves, keeping their salvation in the hands of Son and Spirit.
Henry, with Caryl: if the stars have no light before the sun, what light has the sun before God? (Isa. 24:23).

themes: the brightest creatures dim before God

schools.summary: Clarke argues aph ki should read 'how much less,' and draws the figure of drinking sin like water — the finished portrait of a bad man; Wesley: contracted habits of sinning, drunk as freely as water.
Gill: the descent from greater to less — man loathsome and defiled, naturally and originally filthy, no clean thing from the unclean.
Ellicott judges the strong language meant to reflect on Job in particular; Keil and Delitzsch keep the sweep, 'how much less the abominable and corrupt.'
Henry: if saints and heavens are not pure, much less man; he drinks iniquity as water to a man in a dropsy — the more he sins the more he would.

debates.question: Does the particle aph ki mount to 'how much more' or descend to 'how much less'?

sides.position: 'how much more abominable is man' (the received reading)
'how much less' would God confide in filthy man

themes: how much more abominable is man

schools.summary: Gill: Eliphaz proceeds to defend his proposition — only the wicked are afflicted, and as Job is — promising things worthy of regard, not Job's vain talk.

Henry exposes the false conversion (the wicked are miserable, therefore the miserable wicked) and the pride of a preface that commends its own reasoning and appeals to what Eliphaz has 'himself seen.'
Ellicott hears Eliphaz adopting Bildad's appeal to tradition (ch. 8:8) in an age before civil disturbance; Keil and Delitzsch begin unfolding the poetic portrait of the ungodly man in pain.
Gill: the 'wise men' are wise unto salvation, who would report nothing false, so their tradition from the fathers deserves regard.
Wesley marks 'have not hid it' — the fathers judged the truth too certain and important to conceal.
Henry draws the wholesome lesson of transmitted wisdom (Ps. 78:3-6), even as the doctrine built on it goes astray.

themes: the portrait of the ungodly begins

schools.summary: Clarke leans to Israel receiving the promised land with no stranger suffered in it; Wesley reads a thrust at Job — God so guarded these men no enemy could spoil them, as the Sabeans spoiled Job (confuting ch. 9:24).
Gill takes the 'wise men' for rulers of kingdoms, likely Noah and his sons to whom the whole earth was given after the flood, not the patriarchs in Canaan.
Henry: the authorities were men of rank, favourites of heaven, best fitted to observe God's providences.

debates.question: To whom 'alone the earth was given'?

sides.position: the Israelites in the promised land, no stranger among them
Noah and his sons, to whom the whole earth was given after the flood

themes: unto whom alone the earth was given
a covert rebuke of the plundered Job

schools.summary: Ellicott insists the clause is not independent ('even the number of years laid up for the oppressor'), and paints the tyrant living like Damocles under a hanging sword (cf. ch. 4:12).

Clarke takes mithcholel as 'he torments himself,' a self-tormentor and author of his own ruin; Wesley: a life of care, fear, and grief, the oppressor named because Eliphaz supposed Job guilty of that sin (against ch. 12:6).
Gill weighs the pain as the toil of sinning, the sorrows of getting wealth, or the gripe of conscience — not every wicked man in outward pain.

outliers.note: Records a Targum's strange turn that reads the verse of 'the ungodly Esau,' expected to repent but never repenting, and of 'the sturdy Ishmael' from whom the number of years was hidden.

themes: the wicked man travaileth with pain

schools.summary: Gill distinguishes imaginary fears (Cain, Magor-missabib) from real ones (the Syrian host of 2 Kings 7; the messengers of calamity that dog Job).
Clarke: the oppressor can have no rest, suspecting his cruelties will recoil on himself; Wesley: even feeling no evil he is tormented with perpetual fears, and the destroyer comes suddenly.

themes: a dreadful sound in his ears

schools.summary: Gill allows the graver overtone — a glance at Job's hopelessness, and the heathen Idumeans without hope of resurrection out of the darkness of the grave.
Clarke narrows it to the dread of the assassin's dagger and rejects the resurrection reading as anachronistic; Wesley keeps to the psychology of guilt, the 'sword' any grievous affliction.

debates.question: Does 'return out of darkness' reach to the hope of resurrection?

sides.position: only the fear of the assassin and loss of this life; the resurrection sense is anachronistic
it may reach on to the darkness of the grave and the want of hope beyond it

schools.summary: Clarke paints the reversal from affluence to begging a morsel, with death 'in his hand'; Wesley grounds the knowledge of the coming dark day in the guilty conscience.
Gill hesitates between the roving plunderer and the beggar wandering door to door (the curse of Ps. 109:10).
Ellicott marks the picture as overdrawn and inconsistent — the same man both tyrant and beggar — unless foraging as well as plunder be the raider's object.

outliers.note: Candidly flags the description as internally inconsistent — the prosperous oppressor cannot easily also be a beggar wandering for bread — resolving it only by supposing forage the object of a marauder's raids.

themes: the day of darkness at hand

schools.summary: Clarke: the man's crimes as numerous as a king's troops, yet deserted and slain by them; sealed with Juvenal, that few tyrants die a dry, quiet death.
Gill reads the fear as of worse troubles present, or the wrath, tribulation, and anguish to come on every soul that doeth evil (Rom. 2:9).
Ellicott construes 'they prevail against him like a king,' the man destined to be a ball, the tennis-ball of calamity (Isa. 22:18).

debates.question: How is 'as a king ready to the battle' construed?

sides.position: trouble assaults the man as a king marches out to battle, mighty and prepared
terrors prevail over him as a king overwhelms a beaten foe; he is tossed like a ball

themes: as a king ready to battle
violence the exit of the violent

schools.summary: Ellicott reads the wicked man running on God behind 'the thick bosses of his bucklers,' his own prosperity his false armour (Deut. 32:15; Ps. 17:10), against the AV that makes the armour God's.
Gill: the stretched-out hand is enmity itself against God, the more daring sins striking at his very being (Heb. 10:29).
Clarke: the man in power thought himself supreme, oppressing rather than protecting; Wesley marvels at the madness of the worm fighting the omnipotent God.

debates.question: Whose are 'the thick bosses of the bucklers'?

sides.position: the wicked man's own — his prosperity the false armour behind which he charges God
God's — the Almighty arming himself against the rebel (the Authorized Version)
holders: the Authorized Version (as reported by Ellicott)

themes: stretching out the hand against God

schools.summary: Gill: the wicked man runs upon God as the he-goat on the ram, closing to seize the throat, or charging 'with his neck,' brow like brass.
Wesley reads the man grappling with God at the buckler's strongest point; Clarke, following Calmet, reverses it — God rushes upon the ungodly and seizes his throat, which the mail cannot protect.
Keil and Delitzsch render the man assailing God 'with a stiff neck, with the thick bosses of his shield,' the bucklers his own.

debates.question: Who runs upon whom in 'he runneth upon him, even on his neck'?

sides.position: the wicked man charges God, neck outstretched behind his shield
God, like a conquering hero, rushes upon the wicked man's throat

themes: running upon him on the neck
the thick bosses of the bucklers

schools.summary: Gill: the fatness is overflowing prosperity that makes the man haughty — a Jeshurun who waxed fat and kicked against God (Deut. 32:15).
Wesley makes fat, rich, potent success the reason of his insolence (Ps. 78:31; Jer. 46:21); Clarke: overloaded with flesh, he cannot defend himself against the strong gripe.

outliers.note: Reports an Arabic rendering that turns 'collops of fat on his flanks' into 'he lays the Pleiades upon the Hyades' — a proverb of boundless ambition, likened to the giants piling mountains to scale heaven until Jove's thunderbolt ruins their works.

themes: a covert thrust at Job's former wealth

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch read a divinely-appointed desolation ('ready to become heaps,' cf. Deut. 13:16; 1 Kings 16:34), taking it generally of careless settling without fear of God; Ellicott completes the tyrant's portrait without fixing the tense.
Wesley: the verse begins the description of his misery; Clarke: the tyrant reduced to inhabit the very cities his wars had ruined.
Gill offers first the prosperity sense (per the Targum): his might destroys cities and raises greater on their ruins to perpetuate his name.

debates.question: Is dwelling in desolate cities the wicked man's prosperity or his judgment?

sides.position: his prosperity — he ruins cities and builds greater on the ruins (the Targum)
his judgment — reduced to inhabit ruins, the beginning of his misery

themes: the desolate city his proper dwelling

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott labour over the obscure minlam / 'perfection thereof' (a word found nowhere else), rejecting the older 'extend himself upon the earth' and offering 'their produce shall not bend to the earth.'
Gill: though he labours with all his might he shall not attain riches; some gather much yet grow poor, poorest of all toward God.
Clarke hears the whole passage aimed at Job as a supposed oppressor; Wesley: what he had gotten shall be taken from him.

Clarke reads the drying branches as children cut off and 'the breath of his mouth' as God's destroying blast; Wesley expounds flame as God's judgment, branches as encircling glory, and 'go back' as fleeing God faster than he ran on him (v.26).
Gill lets the darkness deepen from poverty to unforsaken sin to the reserved blackness of darkness.
Ellicott ties it to the darkness of v.22 and reads 'by the breath of his mouth' (cf. ch. 11:20) as the man passing away suddenly, like his own breath.

themes: the breath that carries him off

schools.summary: Gill anatomises the deception — by Satan, by the deceitful heart, by the deceitfulness of sin and riches — and the vanities the man trusts.
Clarke: the seventh evil — trusting in a lie that becomes his recompence; Wesley widens it to a caution for all and plays on 'his exchange,' vanity bartered for vanity.
Ellicott renders 'let him not trust in vanity, deceiving himself' (cf. James 1:26; 1 Sam. 12:21).

themes: the empty thing and the empty reward

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch open the last strophe (the withering branch, the vine casting unripe grapes, the olive shedding its flower); Ellicott reads 'paid in full before its time' and marks how the orthodox saw fails utterly before an innocent sufferer like Job.
Gill: the recompence comes 'before his day,' or the life is cut short before its natural term — an immature death.
Clarke (with the Vulgate): a violent death, not half his days, and no scion from his root; Wesley: cut off when nature might have continued him longer.

themes: the maxim that fails before Job

schools.summary: Gill turns the figure of the shaken vine several ways — the man losing his substance, God shaking off all he held dear, children snatched unripe — and suspects an eye to Job's ruined estate and family.

Clarke reads both figures of the man's posterity, fallen like wind-fall grapes and blasted olive-blossoms; the vine and olive, yielding wine and oil for worship and comfort, apt emblems of a hopeful progeny cut off before it could fulfil expectation.

themes: a reproach aimed at Job's bereavement

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch render 'desolate' as galmud, a hard lifeless stony mass — the ungodly family left barren while fire devours the tents of bribery; Ellicott notes 'desolate' was Job's own uncommon word (ch. 3:7), perhaps an intentional echo.
Gill: the 'congregation of hypocrites' (a form of godliness without power, 2 Tim. 3:5) glances at Job's household, now desolate — or 'solitary,' destitute of friends.
Clarke hears two insinuations against Job — classing him with the impious (the barren rock of ch. 3:7) and hinting he perverted justice and took bribes.

themes: Job's own word turned against him

schools.summary: Clarke draws out the figure of monstrous birth (sin conceived from Satan's seed, travailed with pangs, bringing forth deceit and death, cf. James 1:15), then turns tenderly to 'poor Job,' besieged in body, mind, and heart, yet chained enemies and an unseen Protector.
Gill reads it plainly: the wicked meditate sin, contrive it, and frame schemes to do others mischief.
Keil and Delitzsch confirm the vividness (cf. Ps. 7:14; Isa. 59:4) — they hatch others' sorrow, and what their inward part prepares recoils in evil on themselves.

outliers.note: Breaks from the doctrine to a pastoral aside on 'poor Job' — body wasted, mind harassed by Satan, heart wrung by false friends — insisting his enemies were chained and God his unseen Protector kept him from being greatly moved.

themes: the sufferer under an unseen Protector
